content.introduction: Markets rose significantly in May 2026, with the S&P 500 up 10.5% and emerging markets leading at +14.7%. The strong performance was driven by a rotation into AI stocks and solid economic growth. Despite rising oil prices, the U.S. economy remained resilient.
body: Rising oil prices increased inflationary pressures, reducing expectations for near-term rate cuts despite solid economic growth and leadership changes at the Federal Reserve. Stock investors who either held steady through April’s fluctuations or wrote off the early weeks of our conflict with Iran as a passing or inconsequential phenomenon were rewarded as the S&P 500 rose 10.5%, reversing the losses of March as the year-to-date return bounced back to 5.7%. While oil prices and daily stock valuations fluctuated with the fortunes of war and the oscillating news regarding the Strait of Hormuz, the underlying strength of the U.S. economy, corporate earnings, and labor market supported the steady upward trend for the stock market. Large oil companies stand to join the earnings winners as they benefit from higher crude and gas prices, which could remain elevated for some time, even if the conflict in the Middle East is settled. As higher oil prices percolate through the economy, expectations for future rate cuts have continued to drop, in spite of the shift in leadership at the Federal Reserve.

Global equities staged a powerful risk-on rally, driven by a rotation back into artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq hit all-time highs, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose close to 40% over the month, and the MSCI Emerging Markets Index was the standout index (+14.7%), powered by extraordinary gains in Taiwan (+26.2%) and South Korea (+38.2%), leading markets in the global AI supply chain.

The pattern continues to lean decisively bearish, and the probability of a downside break remains far higher than any meaningful move upward. Price slipped back beneath the wedge structure and closed the week just under the ascending trendline — a level that has now flipped into a clear resistance zone. That’s why I pulled up the monthly chart — it’s the only timeframe that truly captures how remarkably well this structure has held over the years. Adjusting parallel channels is valid as long as the broader narrative and pattern structure remain intact — and in XOM’s case, they clearly do. Moves like this often lead to short‑term downside, though the upward trendline is still intact — meaning a pullback into the low $80s remains entirely possible without breaking the broader structure. McDonald’s remains in a corrective trend, and the chart still reflects a market working through weakness rather than reversing. The chart is holding above its long‑term trend line, which keeps the broader structure constructive.
